content: The ability of various indicators to measure changes in iron status following an iron intervention was evaluated. Based on the analysis of data and expert consultation, it was concluded that hemoglobin concentration should be measured to assess iron status, even though not all anemia cases are caused by iron deficiency. Additionally, the assessment of serum ferritin and soluble transferrin receptor was identified as the most effective approach for evaluating the iron status of populations. When evaluating the impact of interventions aimed at controlling iron deficiency in populations, it was recommended to use serum ferritin as an indicator of response to such interventions. This should be measured alongside hemoglobin concentration in all program evaluations. Furthermore, if funding permits, measuring the concentration of acute-phase proteins, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) or α-1 acid glycoprotein (AGP), may be beneficial to account for elevated serum ferritin levels caused by inflammation. Measuring transferrin receptor levels during repeated surveys was also suggested. In September 2010, the World Health Organization (WHO) convened its first guideline development group meeting in Panama City, Panama, to discuss priorities for assessing vitamin A and iron status in populations. This meeting initiated the process of updating WHO guidelines on indicators for assessing these nutritional statuses. Serum ferritin and soluble transferrin receptor were identified as the highest-priority indicators for a comprehensive review. Starting in 2013, WHO launched a project to retrieve, summarize, and assess evidence to inform recommendations on the use and interpretation of serum/plasma ferritin concentrations for assessing iron status in populations. Five protocols were developed to address specific topics through systematic reviews of published data and analyses of raw data from international databases. These protocols included: 1. Serum/plasma ferritin for assessing iron status in populations: This protocol examined whether ferritin concentration reflects all possible iron statuses (deficiency, repletion, and overload) and identified appropriate cut-off points for defining each status. It also explored the association of serum/plasma ferritin with other measures of iron stores, such as bone marrow aspirates, hemoglobin, blood smears, and liver biopsies. 2. How ferritin concentration responds to nutrition interventions: This protocol summarized systematic reviews assessing the effects of nutrition-specific and nutrition-sensitive interventions on ferritin concentrations, particularly in children aged 6–59 months, school-aged children, and pregnant and non-pregnant women of reproductive age. 3. The accuracy and comparability of methods for measuring ferritin concentration: This protocol reviewed different laboratory methods for assessing ferritin concentration and aimed to estimate adjustments needed between methods, if necessary. 4. The influence of inflammation on ferritin concentrations: This protocol used a methodological approach to adjust ferritin values in population-based surveys. It aimed to describe and compare approaches for accounting for inflammation using acute-phase protein measurements, identifying the most accurate and practical method for describing the prevalence of low ferritin. 5. The use of ferritin concentrations in defining levels of public health concern regarding iron status in populations: This protocol aimed to describe the magnitude and distribution of iron deficiency, as measured by ferritin concentration, across different regions of the world. It sought to inform guidelines and define ranges, severities, and proportions of iron deficiency at national or regional levels. In March 2014, WHO, in collaboration with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), held a technical consultation at Emory University in Atlanta, USA, to validate the methodological approach for retrieving, summarizing, and assessing evidence to inform future guidelines on ferritin use as an indicator of iron status. Experts in ferritin methodology, immunology, nutrition, and program implementation met with authors of meta-analyses to discuss draft review protocols and preliminary results. Subsequent meetings were held in Geneva, Switzerland (December 2014), Bethesda, USA (May 2015), and Geneva again (March 2016) to present and discuss the results of the reviews, develop draft recommendations, and finalize WHO guidelines on the use of ferritin concentrations to assess iron status in populations. The final guideline development group meeting took place in Geneva in June 2016, where evidence was presented, recommendations were finalized, and the strength of the recommendations was determined, considering costs, values, preferences, and implementation challenges. The importance of developing this guideline aligns with WHO’s 13th General Programme of Work (GPW13) for 2019–2023, which focuses on achieving universal health coverage, addressing health emergencies, and promoting healthier populations. Accurate determination of iron status is critical for both clinical and public health purposes. At the individual level, diagnosing iron deficiency or overload guides management, further investigations, and appropriate therapy. At the population level, understanding the magnitude and distribution of iron deficiency helps prioritize interventions in areas with severe public health problems or identify populations at risk of hereditary conditions predisposing them to iron overload. In support of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the United Nations Decade of Action on Nutrition (2016–2025), WHO aims to advance nutrition through leadership, guidance, and monitoring. This includes accelerating progress toward achieving global nutrition targets and addressing key areas such as guidance, policy, surveillance, and engagement to promote universal health coverage and healthier populations. The evidence informing the recommendations on ferritin as a marker of iron stores is based on three systematic reviews. These reviews assessed the diagnostic accuracy of ferritin compared to gold standards, identified appropriate cut-off values for defining deficiency and excess, and evaluated the most commonly used ferritin thresholds in pregnant women. The findings highlighted the need for unified international thresholds for iron deficiency during pregnancy and emphasized the importance of accounting for inflammation when interpreting ferritin concentrations.
